requirements.requirement: Application data under /srv/data made recoverable through filesystem snapshots (baseline snapshot capability established)
requirements.summary: A btrfs filesystem was created and mounted at /srv/data, populated with application data (config, db, log files), and a read-only snapshot 'snapshots/baseline' was taken with a recorded SHA-256 manifest, directly demonstrating snapshot-based recoverability.

requirements.requirement: Directory /srv/data is modified after the snapshot is captured
requirements.summary: After the baseline snapshot, the config file was edited, data.csv was deleted, and a new file was added; a manifest diff directly confirmed the divergence from the baseline.

requirements.requirement: Restore /srv/data to the exact content captured by the earlier snapshot
requirements.summary: The live 'current' subvolume was deleted and recreated as a writable snapshot of 'baseline', remounted at /srv/data, and a SHA-256 manifest diff showed zero differences from the baseline, directly confirming exact restoration.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed on node1 with pre-restart baseline, acknowledgement, changed boot identity, and recovered service/data state
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id and /srv/data health/checksums were captured, systemctl reboot was issued with an ack before disconnect, a later poll confirmed a new boot_id, and post-restart checks showed /srv/data auto-remounted via fstab with both btrfs subvolumes intact and checksums matching the pre-restart baseline exactly. This is corroborated by the fixed lifecycle boot-identity observations (fe422859... before, 9114851d... after).

overall_summary: The executor established btrfs-backed snapshot recoverability for /srv/data on node1 in the absence of LVM/rsync, took a baseline snapshot, modified the data, and restored it to an exact match of the baseline via SHA-256 manifest verification—directly satisfying the task's core contract. The mandatory node-restart evidence protocol was also completed with direct, coherent evidence of pre-restart health, reboot acknowledgement, boot identity change, and post-restart data/mount recovery, cross-checked against the fixed lifecycle boot-identity snapshots. Hygiene is good with only minor uncleaned temp manifest/log files as residue.
limitations: Package-health checks in the fixed lifecycle snapshots were unavailable (timed out) both before and after, so package consistency state could not be independently cross-checked, though this is unrelated to the task's file-level outcomes.
A handful of manifest and log files were left in /tmp after task completion; this is low-risk residue not explicitly cleaned up by the executor.

operational_hygiene.summary: Command timeline reviewed chronologically: early discovery commands (os/disk/lvm/yum checks) were read-only or failed without state mutation (e.g., checking for a stale yum lock found none to remove; failed yum install attempts due to disabled repos made no changes). The modprobe btrfs load was a necessary prerequisite for the chosen snapshot mechanism given the absence of LVM/rsync/yum repos. No unnecessary or unreverted mutations were found tied to abandoned troubleshooting paths. The only minor residue is a handful of manifest/log files left in /tmp (baseline_manifest.txt, modified_manifest.txt, postreboot_manifest.txt, restored_manifest.txt, reboot.log), visible in the after-executor temporary-files diff; this is bounded, low-risk residue rather than a harmful or destructive mutation.
